https://www.perl.com/pub/2004/04/16/a12..says: Adopts the Traits paper's case for separating object management from code reuse and cites only that paper, but lets roles carry state, rejects renaming or excluding conflicting methods, and allows runtime mixins.

https://wiki.php.net/rfc/horizontalreuse.who: Stefan Marr, author of PHP's traits RFC
https://wiki.php.net/rfc/horizontalreuse.where: PHP RFC: Horizontal Reuse for PHP
https://wiki.php.net/rfc/horizontalreuse.says: Lists Perl 6 among earlier adopters of traits, beside Scala, Squeak, Fortress, Slate and Self, and takes its bibliography from the Bern Traits papers; the traits part shipped in PHP 5.4.

https://person.dibris.unige.it/zucca-ele.who: Brian Goetz, Java language architect at Oracle
https://person.dibris.unige.it/zucca-ele.says: Presents Java's planned default methods as a restricted, stateless kind of traits, chosen because full traits were too large a change, with conflicting defaults left for the programmer to resolve explicitly.

https://web.archive.org/web/2019/https:/.where: Perl 6 RFC 256, Objects: Native support for multimethods
https://web.archive.org/web/2019/https:/.says: Proposes built-in multimethod dispatch for Perl 6, contrasting the approach CLOS takes and pointing readers to his own Class::Multimethods module.

https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1209.5.who: Jeff Bezanson, Stefan Karpinski, Viral Shah and Alan Edelman, Julia's creators
https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1209.5.where: arXiv 1209.5145, Julia: A Fast Dynamic Language for Technical Computing
https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1209.5.says: Places Julia's generic functions in the tradition of CLOS and Dylan and alongside Cecil and Diesel, makes them its main abstraction mechanism, and never mentions Perl.

https://web.archive.org/web/2012/http://.where: Perl 6 RFC 82, Arrays: Apply operators element-wise in a list context
https://web.archive.org/web/2012/http://.says: Proposes that operators act on lists element by element, giving the Perl Data Language and Numerical Python's array operations as its references.

https://www.nntp.perl.org/group/perl.per.says: Decides to keep French quotes for word lists and to write vector multiplication as »*«, with >>*<< for ASCII-only text and the bitshift operators renamed to make room.

https://github.com/Raku/mu/commit/088e2d.where: S03 version 59, Pugs svn r11969 (Raku/mu mirror)
https://github.com/Raku/mu/commit/088e2d.says: Adds X to S03 as a fifth metaoperator that pairs every element of one list with every element of the others, and lets a bare X serve as an operator itself.

https://julialang.org/blog/2017/01/mored.where: Julia blog, More Dots: Syntactic Loop Fusion in Julia
https://julialang.org/blog/2017/01/mored.says: Describes Julia 0.6's fusing dot syntax for vectorized code, naming Matlab, NumPy and R as where that style is familiar and contrasting Chapel's automatic vectorization; Perl is not mentioned.

https://web.archive.org/web/2019/https:/.where: Perl 6 RFC 81, Lazily evaluated list generation functions
https://web.archive.org/web/2019/https:/.says: Proposes lazily generated lists, pointing to Haskell's and Python 2's list comprehensions and to the range syntax used in Matlab and IDL.

https://peps.python.org/pep-0255/.who: Neil Schemenauer, Tim Peters and Magnus Lie Hetland, PEP authors
https://peps.python.org/pep-0255/.says: Credits Sather's iterators, themselves derived from CLU, and Icon's generators as precedents for Python generators; Perl is not mentioned.
https://peps.python.org/pep-0255/.quote: Some other high-level languages provide pleasant solutions, notably iterators in Sather, which were inspired by iterators in CLU; and generators in Icon, a novel language where every expression is a generator.
https://peps.python.org/pep-0255/.rest: The passage goes on to the idea they share: a function that hands its caller the next value and keeps its local state, so it can resume where it left off. Perl appears nowhere in the PEP.

https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3513-ge.says: Surveys generator designs as prior art, from CLU, Icon and Python to Kotlin, Swift, C# and Koka, without mentioning Perl or Raku.

https://www.perl.com/pub/2003/03/07/apoc.says: Introduces the ==> and <== pipe operators for feeding lists, likening list operators to Unix commands that pass streams of data through pipes.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archiv.says: Traces F#'s pipeline operator to Isabelle/ML, publishing April–May 1994 emails among Paulson, Nipkow and Wenzel in which Tobias Nipkow settled on the |> name.

https://digitalmars.com/d/1.0/changelog2.says: Lists scope statements as new in DMD 0.148, then records that 0.149 respelled the three on_scope_* forms as scope(exit), scope(success) and scope(failure).

https://forum.dlang.org/post/du106f$ptt$.says: Introducing scope guards, says the design derives from macros Andrei Alexandrescu wrote for C++ and describes it as something no other language offers.

https://github.com/golang/go/commit/4a90.who: Robert Griesemer, Go co-designer (reviewed by Rob Pike)
https://github.com/golang/go/commit/4a90.says: Adds defer to the Go spec as a call postponed until the enclosing function returns, with its arguments evaluated at once and pending calls run last-in, first-out.

https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/.where: Error Handling Rationale and Proposal, swift/docs
https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/.says: Recommends that Swift adopt Go's defer in preference to Java's try/finally, but run deferred actions when their scope ends rather than when the function returns.

https://andrewkelley.me/post/zig-january.says: Reports swapping Zig's error-handling sigils for keywords after newcomers complained, so that %defer became errdefer and %return became try.

https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/.who: Jens Gustedt and Robert C. Seacord, WG14 paper authors
https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/.where: WG14 N2895, A simple defer feature for C
https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/.says: Proposes a defer feature for C modelled on Go's, with POSIX cleanup handlers, MSVC __try/__finally and GCC's cleanup attribute as existing practice; Perl is not mentioned.

https://github.com/elixir-lang/elixir/bl.says: Records that String.length, String.at and related functions now operate on graphemes.

https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/.who: Dave Abrahams and Ben Cohen, Swift standard library team
https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/.where: String Processing For Swift 4 (String Manifesto), swift/docs
https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/.says: Grounds Swift 4's string redesign in Unicode grapheme clusters as defined by UAX #29 and mentions Perl only as the string-processing benchmark to beat; Perl 6 and NFG never appear.

https://perl6advent.wordpress.com/2013/1.says: Introduces Supplies as Perl 6's built-in support for reactive programming, tracing the idea from the duality of observers and iterators through the Rx library.

https://peps.python.org/pep-0492/.where: PEP 492, Coroutines with async and await syntax
https://peps.python.org/pep-0492/.says: Gives C#, the async functions proposed for ECMAScript 7, Hack, Dart and Scala as precedents for async/await; Perl is absent.
https://peps.python.org/pep-0492/.quote: async/await is not a new concept in programming languages: C# has it since long time ago; proposal to add async/await in ECMAScript 7; see also Traceur project; Facebook's Hack/HHVM; Google's Dart language; Scala; proposal to add async/await to C++; and many other less popular languages.
https://peps.python.org/pep-0492/.rest: The PEP counts that familiarity as a benefit to programmers who already use async/await elsewhere. Perl appears nowhere in it.

https://peps.python.org/pep-0635/.who: Tobias Kohn and Guido van Rossum, PEP authors
https://peps.python.org/pep-0635/.where: PEP 635, Structural Pattern Matching: Motivation and Rationale
https://peps.python.org/pep-0635/.says: Surveys pattern matching in thirteen languages, among them Haskell, Scala, Rust, Erlang and F#, and never mentions Perl.
https://peps.python.org/pep-0635/.quote: In addition, this would put Python in a rather unique position: The underscore is as a wildcard pattern in every programming language with pattern matching that we could find (including C#, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Grace, Haskell, Mathematica, OCaml, Ruby, Rust, Scala, Swift, and Thorn).
https://peps.python.org/pep-0635/.rest: The passage defends `_` as the wildcard: choosing anything else is what would make Python the odd one out. The motivation section names Haskell, Erlang, Scala, Elixir, Ruby and a JavaScript proposal; Perl appears nowhere in the PEP.

https://openjdk.org/jeps/441.says: Extends Java's switch to test a value against patterns, finalizing the feature for Java 21, and names no other language as a model.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Void_safet.says: Credits Bertrand Meyer with the term void safety, dates Eiffel's attached types to ECOOP 2005, and says Ceylon has had union-type null safety since 2011.

https://www.python.org/download/releases.where: Unifying types and classes in Python 2.2, python.org
https://www.python.org/download/releases.says: Explains Python 2.2's new metaclasses and method resolution order, crediting the Forman and Danforth book Putting Metaclasses to Work for the MRO change and for the term cooperative method.

https://metacpan.org/pod/Class::C3.says: Traces C3 from Dylan through Python 2.3 and reports that Perl 6 chose it as the standard MRO for classes and Parrot as its default for objects.

https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/.says: Calls metaprogramming Lisp's strongest legacy in Julia, offering true Lisp-style macros that work on abstract syntax trees.

https://github.com/Raku/old-design-docs/.says: Makes a first attempt in S02 at explaining how several languages are braided into one program, the first time the words slang and braid appear in the spec repository.

https://bford.info/pub/lang/peg.pdf.where: Parsing Expression Grammars: A Recognition-Based Syntactic Foundation, POPL 2004
https://bford.info/pub/lang/peg.pdf.says: Defines parsing expression grammars, tracing them to Birman's TS/TDPL and gTS/GTDPL formalisms and to Aho and Ullman, and never mentions Perl.

https://github.com/Raku/old-design-docs/.says: Adds to S05 an overview describing Perl 6 patterns as a native implementation of parsing expression grammars, together with explicit tiebreaking rules.

https://www.inf.puc-rio.br/~roberto/docs.where: A Text Pattern-Matching Tool based on Parsing Expression Grammars (LPeg paper)
https://www.inf.puc-rio.br/~roberto/docs.says: Presents LPeg as a PEG-based matcher whose first-class pattern style comes from SNOBOL4; its Perl references concern only Perl 5 regexes and a benchmark.

https://groups.google.com/g/perl.perl6.l.who: Larry Wall, Perl 6 language designer, replying to Stéphane Payrard
https://groups.google.com/g/perl.perl6.l.says: Answering a remark that the Smalltalk traits paper made roles stateless, notes its authors meant to study state and says a role may also supply attributes.

https://scg.unibe.ch/archive/papers/Duca.who: Stéphane Ducasse, Oscar Nierstrasz, Nathanael Schärli, Roel Wuyts and Andrew Black, the Traits authors
https://scg.unibe.ch/archive/papers/Duca.where: ACM TOPLAS 28(2), Traits: A Mechanism for Fine-Grained Reuse
https://scg.unibe.ch/archive/papers/Duca.says: Lists traits as standard in Scala and implemented for Perl 5, and reports work under way to build them into Perl 6, where they are called roles.

https://groups.google.com/g/julia-dev/c/.says: Says resembling CLOS was never a goal for Julia and that its likeness to Fortress arose because both languages faced similar problems rather than from mutual inspiration.

https://www.perl.com/pub/2001/10/02/apoc.says: Accepts RFC 82's element-wise operators as hyper operators marked by a leading caret, joking that APL is next, and has them stretch a scalar across a missing dimension.

https://www.perl.com/pub/2002/01/15/apo4.says: Specifies KEEP blocks that run only on success and UNDO blocks only on failure, pairs POST with PRE for design by contract, and renames switch/case to given/when after discussion with Conway.

https://forum.dlang.org/post/9lsnrc$1kdo.says: When asked if D borrowed from Perl 6's design, replies that he has not followed Perl 6, so any resemblance is coincidence.

https://github.com/golang/go/commit/1593.says: A tidy-up of the Go spec's open items keeps an entry noting that the language still lacks an onreturn/undo statement.

https://github.com/Perl/PPCs/blob/main/p.says: Explains the block was first named LEAVE, dropped because Raku's LEAVE behaves differently, and that Raku's phaser blocks take effect at compile time merely by being declared, whereas defer acts only once execution reaches it.

https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/docume.says: States that each Swift Character value represents one extended grapheme cluster.

https://forums.swift.org/t/declarative-s.who: Michael Ilseman, Apple's String and regex lead
https://forums.swift.org/t/declarative-s.where: Swift Forums, Declarative String Processing Overview, post 100
https://forums.swift.org/t/declarative-s.says: Notes that certain regex engines can match by canonical equivalence or by grapheme clusters, adding that he believes Perl 6 did.

https://github.com/MoarVM/MoarVM/blob/nq.says: Describes MoarVM's NFG string form, which extends Unicode NFC, held in fixed-width arrays where negative values stand for synthetic graphemes of several codepoints.

https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/pull/.says: Rejects NFG-style synthetic graphemes for Julia, arguing they suit only strings that start as UTF-32, not UTF-8, and waste a great deal of memory.
Tells the Julia developers that Parrot's PDD 28 string design had always been aspirational and only loosely shaped the Rakudo and MoarVM implementation.

https://github.com/Raku/old-design-docs/.says: Adds the Int:D type modifier to S12, restricting a parameter or variable to defined Int instances.

https://metacpan.org/pod/Quantum::Superp.says: Adds any and all operators to Perl 5 that merge several values into one superposed scalar; Perl 6 goes unmentioned in its documentation.

https://web.archive.org/web/2012/http://.says: Proposes, in earnest, any and all operators that give Perl 6 superposition types, and points readers to the Quantum::Superpositions module.

https://metacpan.org/pod/Switch.says: Provides a switch statement for Perl 5; later releases note that Perl 6 will spell it given and when and offer a Perl6 mode using those keywords.

https://web.archive.org/web/2019/https:/.says: Proposes a built-in reduce for Perl 6, modelled on the reduce subroutine in Graham Barr's List::Util module.

https://web.archive.org/web/2019/https:/.where: Perl 6 RFC 271, Subroutines: Pre- and post- handlers for subroutines
https://web.archive.org/web/2019/https:/.says: Proposes pre- and post-handlers for subroutines, extending the approach of his Class::Contract module to a general mechanism for handlers.
Proposes the ^_ placeholder as a cleaner way to create curried, higher-order functions, citing a Haskell tutorial as an existing implementation.

https://www.perl.com/pub/2002/06/04/apo5.says: Calls its backtracking controls variants of Prolog's cut, and says a proposal for matching on Perl data structures reminds Wall of Prolog unification.

https://www.nntp.perl.org/group/perl.per.says: Proposes that double-quoted strings interpolate only backslash escapes, variables with subscripts and {EXPR} closures, so method calls need braces, a change he jokes turns up the Ruby-o-meter.

https://developers.slashdot.org/story/16.who: Larry Wall, interviewed by Slashdot readers
https://developers.slashdot.org/story/16.where: The Slashdot Interview With Larry Wall
https://developers.slashdot.org/story/16.says: Says other languages took Perl 5's regexes, jokes that a PHP borrowing enough to be consistent would have reimplemented Perl 6, and credits C#, Erlang, Go and Haskell for Perl 6's concurrency ideas.

https://github.com/Perl/PPCs/blob/main/p.where: Perl PPC 0027, More list processing operators inspired by List::Util
https://github.com/Perl/PPCs/blob/main/p.says: Adds any and all list keywords modelled on List::Util, and rejects making them junctions, since junction values need no special syntax and can live in ordinary modules.

https://forums.swift.org/t/pitch-simplif.says: Likens the pitch to Raku junctions and advises against them, citing hidden loops that obscure time complexity and harm to type-checking, and suggests shipping a package instead.

https://github.com/fsharp/fslang-suggest.says: Declines the suggestion, saying F# itself will not add it because programmers already have several ways to express it; a 2018 commenter had likened it to a Perl 6 junction.

https://externals.io/message/92857#92870.says: Wishes PHP had something like Perl 6 junctions, giving an instanceof test against any of several classes as an example.

https://forum.dlang.org/post/igcoqh$1tir.says: Reports an attempt to implement Perl 6-style junctions in D as a library.

https://github.com/ghc-proposals/ghc-pro.says: Floats an explicit marker for Haskell tuple sections, citing Raku's Whatever star beside placeholders in Scala, Lean, C++, Mathematica and PureScript as prior art.

https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/propos.where: Rust internals forum, Proposal: Grammar Working Group, post 8
https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/propos.says: Describes the separator forms of the proposed grammar notation, written with %, attributing that syntax to Perl 6 from memory and crediting eternaleye with suggesting it.

https://github.com/Kotlin/KEEP/blob/mast.who: Andrey Breslav and Roman Elizarov, Kotlin language designers
https://github.com/Kotlin/KEEP/blob/mast.where: Kotlin KEEP, Kotlin Coroutines design proposal
https://github.com/Kotlin/KEEP/blob/mast.says: Cites C# and Python for yield-based lazy sequences and C# and JavaScript for async/await, and builds sequence {} on restricted suspension; Perl is never mentioned.
